items: What is the trend on the weekly chart? Are we WITH it?
What is the key support or resistance level nearest to entry?
Is there a candle signal — doji, engulfing, hammer — confirming?
Does an indicator (RSI, MACD, BB) support the same direction?
Where exactly is my stop-loss, and why is it there?
Where is my target, and is R:R at least 2:1?
Am I risking more than 2% of capital on this trade?
Is volume confirming this move, or is it suspiciously low?
Every candle = Open, High, Low, Close — a complete battle report
Doji = indecision; Hammer = demand at lows (only in downtrend)
Engulfing & Three White Soldiers = momentum shift with force
Morning Star / Evening Star = three-candle trend reversals
Support & Resistance: price has memory — these levels repeat
H&S, Double Top, Flag, Triangle all carry measured-move targets
Indicators (RSI, MACD, BB, Volume) CONFIRM — they don't predict
Confluence: stack 3–4 signals before acting. Risk: 2:1 R:R minimum
props.closer: Charts don't lie — but they speak in probabilities, not certainties. Learn the language.

captions: Every price — every candle — is a vote.
Bulls vote up, bears vote down.
The chart is the running tally.
This course: candle anatomy, candlestick patterns,
chart formations, and confirming indicators — end to end.
One note: technical analysis reads probabilities,
not certainties.
These are patterns, not guarantees.
Education only, not investment advice.
Consult a SEBI-registered advisor before investing.
Part one.
The language of charts —
why price tells the story before the headlines do.
Why bother with charts?
By the time a story breaks in the press,
the smart money has already acted.
The chart recorded every transaction in real time —
every buyer, every seller, every institutional order.
Look at the two panels.
The analyst consensus said buy.
What did price actually do?
It broke support, expanded on red days,
and diverged on momentum.
The chart was not wrong.
Price already had the information.
Our job is to learn to read it.
The same stock looks different on different timeframes.
The one-hour chart is noisy — hard to read any direction.
The daily shows a cleaner trend.
The weekly?
The move is unmistakable.
Use the larger timeframe for your directional bias,
the daily for your setup,
and intraday only for precise entry.
Trade WITH the larger timeframe.
Fighting the weekly trend on a one-hour chart is one of the most expensive mistakes a beginner makes.
Every candle has four data points: Open, High, Low,
and Close.
The body spans Open to Close.
Green means Close is above Open — bulls won the session.
The upper wick shows how high price went — then pulled back.
Sellers stepped in at the tip and pushed price back down.
The lower wick shows how low price went — then recovered.
Buyers stepped in and defended that level.
One candle encodes a complete battle: where the session started,
how far each side pushed, and who had the final say.
The close is the verdict.
Part two.
Single candle patterns —
what one candle can tell you about the battle.
The doji: open and close are nearly identical —
paper-thin body.
Neither side won.
Standard doji has equal wicks — pure indecision.
Dragonfly doji: long lower wick, no upper.
Bears pushed hard,
buyers absorbed everything and closed price back at the open.
Demand at lows.
Gravestone: bulls pushed high, then sellers dragged it back.
Long-legged: both sides tried and failed.
Maximum uncertainty.
Context matters —
a doji after a long trend is far more significant.
Hammer: small body at the TOP of the range, long lower wick —
at least twice the body.
Sellers drove price sharply lower —
but buyers absorbed everything and drove it back up.
A sign of demand.
The hammer only matters in a DOWNTREND.
Left panel: five red candles, then the hammer.
Potential reversal.
Right panel: the identical shape in an uptrend —
the Hanging Man.
Same body, same wick, opposite meaning.
After a rally, a long lower wick says bulls had trouble,
not strength.
Context decides everything.
If a doji shows indecision,
a Marubozu shows the opposite: total conviction.
Bullish Marubozu: no wicks.
Open equals Low, Close equals High.
From first tick to last, bulls controlled every moment.
Not a single seller could push it back.
Bearish Marubozu: no wicks.
Open equals High, Close equals Low.
Bears owned the entire session.
A Marubozu at a key breakout level signals strong follow-through intent.
There was no hesitation.
The engulfing pattern shows a clear shift in who controls the market.
Left panel: a small red candle,
then a much larger green candle whose body completely covers the previous body.
Bullish engulfing — buyers came in with overwhelming force.
Right panel: a small green candle,
then a large red candle that swallows it whole.
Bearish engulfing — sellers took the full range and more.
The second body must fully cover the first.
It's most significant after an extended trend —
the bigger the momentum shift, the cleaner the signal.
Part three.
Multi-candle patterns —
when two or three candles together tell a stronger story.
Harami means 'pregnant' in Japanese — a large mother candle,
a small baby nestled inside it.
Bullish harami: a large bearish candle followed by a smaller bullish candle whose body fits entirely within the mother's body.
The prior downward momentum has stalled.
Selling pressure is narrowing.
Bearish harami is the inverse: an uptrend,
a large bullish candle,
then a small bearish candle inside it.
Buying momentum is drying up.
Harami is an alert, not a signal.
Wait for confirmation on the next candle.
Morning Star: three candles,
one of the most reliable bullish reversals.
Candle one: strong bearish — trend clearly down.
Candle two: small body or doji —
selling has exhausted itself.
Candle three: strong bullish,
closing well into the body of the first candle.
Bulls have taken control.
Most powerful when the second candle gaps from the first,
and the third closes more than halfway into the first's body.
Evening Star is the mirror: the same three-candle structure at the top of an uptrend.
Three White Soldiers is a momentum continuation signal —
not a reversal.
Three consecutive bullish candles,
each opening within the previous body and closing near its own high.
A staircase of buying pressure across three sessions.
Three Black Crows is the same structure inverted: three consecutive bearish candles stepping down,
each opening inside the previous body and closing near the low.
Strong distribution.
When Three Black Crows appears after a long rally,
treat it as a serious warning.
Part four.
Chart patterns —
formations that develop over days and weeks and carry measured-move targets.
Support is a price level where buyers historically step in.
Resistance is the ceiling where sellers consistently appear.
Watch the chart: each time price approaches resistance,
it stalls and reverses.
Each test of support finds buyers.
These levels have memory.
The more times a level holds,
the more significant it becomes.
And when price breaks cleanly ABOVE resistance —
that resistance often flips and becomes the new support.
Former resistance becomes support on a retest.
This flip is one of the most reliable phenomena in all of technical analysis.
A trendline connects the lows of an uptrend —
or the highs of a downtrend — into a straight line.
In an uptrend: higher highs AND higher lows.
Each pullback finds support at a higher point than the last.
Connect those higher lows — that's your uptrend line.
As long as price stays above the line, the trend is intact.
Traders buy dips to the line.
A close BELOW the trendline is the first warning.
A second close below confirms the break.
You need at least two points to draw a trendline.
Three touches make it significant.
Head and Shoulders is one of the most reliable reversal patterns.
Three parts: a rally to a peak and pullback —
the left shoulder.
A higher peak — the head.
A third rally that fails to reach the head —
the right shoulder.
The neckline connects the two pullback lows.
Break below the neckline confirms the pattern.
Measured move: head minus neckline,
projected below the breakdown.
Here — head at one eighteen, neckline at one oh three —
target is eighty-eight.
The double top — two roughly equal peaks,
separated by a pullback.
The shape of the letter M.
Price rallied to a peak, was rejected,
pulled back to the neckline,
then rallied again to the same height.
The second time, sellers were ready.
When price breaks below the neckline, the pattern confirms.
Target: project the height from neckline to peaks,
downward from the breakdown.
The double bottom — the letter W —
is the mirror: two equal lows, breakout above the neckline,
same measured move going up.
The bull flag is a continuation pattern —
the trend isn't over, just pausing.
Two parts.
Flagpole: a sharp, strong move up with high volume.
Then the flag: a slow, tight pullback in a downward channel,
on declining volume.
Bulls are resting, not retreating.
Breakout above the flag's upper channel line resumes the prior trend.
Volume should surge on breakout — that's the confirmation.
Target: flagpole height added to the breakout point.
Bear flag is the same structure inverted — sharp move down,
tight upward consolidation, then continuation lower.
The ascending triangle shows buyers getting stronger while sellers hold the same level.
A flat resistance line at the top — price tests it,
gets rejected, pulls back, and tests again.
Same ceiling every time.
But the lows keep rising: each pullback finds support at a HIGHER level.
Higher lows mean buyers are becoming more aggressive.
As the lines converge, the setup coils.
Eventually resistance gives way —
and the move is often sharp and fast.
Descending triangle: flat support, falling highs —
sellers more aggressive.
Usually resolves downward.
Part five.
Indicators —
tools that confirm what price action is already saying.
Never use them instead of price — use them alongside it.
Before RSI, before MACD — there's volume.
Volume is the number of shares traded in a session.
A price move with high volume is meaningful.
On low volume — it's suspect.
Heavy green volume on up days means large buyers are accumulating.
Heavy red volume on down days means distribution.
Classic warning: price making new highs but volume shrinking.
The rally is running out of fuel.
On-Balance Volume adds volume on up days and subtracts on down days.
The OBV line tracks whether money is flowing in or out over time.
A moving average smooths price noise by averaging closes over N periods.
SMA ten: last ten closes averaged.
SMA thirty: slower and smoother.
When the faster SMA ten crosses above SMA thirty,
recent momentum has shifted upward — the golden cross.
Bullish signal.
Death cross: faster MA crossing below the slower.
Bearish momentum.
EMA weights recent prices more heavily — reacts faster.
Short-term traders prefer EMAs; position traders use simple MAs.
Moving averages lag.
They confirm trends after they start.
Use alongside price action.
RSI measures the speed and size of recent price moves,
on a scale of zero to one hundred.
Above seventy: overbought.
Below thirty: oversold.
But in a STRONG uptrend,
RSI can stay above seventy for weeks.
Selling just because RSI is high is one of the most expensive mistakes in trading.
The more powerful use: divergence.
Price makes a higher high, RSI makes a lower high —
momentum is weakening before price confirms it.
That warns of a potential reversal.
Use RSI to confirm a setup.
Not to create one on its own.
MACD is built from three components: the MACD line —
gap between a twelve and twenty-six period EMA.
The signal line — a nine-period EMA of the MACD line.
The histogram — gap between the two.
Key signal: MACD line crossing above the signal line means short-term momentum has turned bullish.
Crossing below — bearish.
The histogram turning positive is often the earliest sign of the cross.
Watch for it flipping near a support level.
MACD is lagging.
It confirms momentum has shifted — not where price will go.
Combine with support, resistance, and candle signals.
Bollinger Bands: a dynamic volatility envelope.
Middle band — twenty-period moving average.
Upper and lower bands — two standard deviations away.
When bands squeeze together,
the market is coiling for a big move.
Direction unknown until price breaks.
After the squeeze, bands expand rapidly.
Initial breakout direction usually tells you where the move goes.
Touching the upper band does NOT mean sell.
In a strong trend, price walks the band.
Confirm with candle or RSI.
Part six.
Putting it all together — confluence, risk management,
and the ritual before every trade.
No single signal is reliable enough to trade on its own.
The power comes from confluence —
multiple signals pointing the same way.
Look at the example: a support zone that has held three times.
A bullish doji at that support.
RSI entering oversold for the first time in weeks.
A volume spike suggesting big buyers.
Price touching the two-hundred-day moving average.
Any one factor alone — maybe.
All five together at the same price level?
That's a high-probability setup.
Stack three or four confluent signals before entering.
Fewer is noise.
Even the best setup fails sometimes.
Risk management is how you stay in the game.
Every trade needs three levels defined BEFORE entry: Entry,
Stop-loss, and Target.
Entry at one hundred, stop at ninety-six —
four points of risk, one R.
Target at one oh eight — eight points of reward, two R.
Risk-to-reward: two to one.
At two-to-one R:R,
you only need to win thirty-four percent of the time to be profitable long-term.
You can lose two out of three trades and still make money if winners are twice your losers.
Position sizing: never risk more than one to two percent of total capital per trade.
Before every trade, run this checklist.
What is the weekly trend — are you trading with it?
Is there a candle signal confirming?
Does an indicator agree?
Where is your stop — at a logical level, not a random number?
Is R:R at least two to one?
Are you risking more than two percent of capital?
Is volume confirming?
If you can't answer confidently — the setup isn't ready.
Wait.
Capital you protect today is ammunition for the setups that ARE ready.
The whole map.
Doji: indecision.
Hammer: demand at lows — only in a downtrend.
Engulfing: momentum shift with force.
Morning Star: three-candle reversal warning.
Support and resistance have memory.
H&S, double tops, flags, triangles —
all have measured-move targets.
Indicators confirm price — RSI, MACD, Bollinger Bands,
volume.
They do not replace price action.
Before every trade: stack confluent signals,
define stop and target first, two-to-one R:R minimum,
two percent max risk per trade.
These tools read probabilities, not certainties.
Education only, not advice.
Consult a SEBI-registered advisor.
Thanks for watching.
